claims.text: Adding 1–3 at.% of a minor alloying element capable of favorable bonding with phosphorus will promote phosphorus-rich chemical short-range ordering.
Phosphorus-rich chemically ordered clusters will retard crystallization.
Retarding crystallization through phosphorus-rich clustering will enhance glass-forming ability.
Retarding crystallization through phosphorus-rich clustering will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The intervention should be effective when the baseline processing already produces an amorphous or near-amorphous structure.
Maintaining the additive concentration around 1–3 at.% is expected to favor the proposed stabilization.
Excessive additive concentrations may fail to stabilize the amorphous state.
Conditions that promote phase separation may prevent the desired stabilization.
Phosphorus-rich chemically short-range ordered clusters act as kinetic barriers to crystalline nucleation.
Interaction between the additive and phosphorus lowers local atomic mobility.
Interaction between the additive and phosphorus increases the energy barrier for crystalline nucleation.
The modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for amorphization than the additive-free baseline.
The modified alloy will have a higher onset crystallization temperature than the additive-free baseline.
The modified alloy will have a wider thermal-stability window for the amorphous state than the additive-free baseline.
The beneficial effect depends on the additive remaining homogeneously distributed and forming stable phosphorus-related clusters.
Additive segregation or formation of separate crystalline phases may degrade glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability.
